key_terms.meaning: A group of equal nodes that connect directly and share data without a central server.
A node forwards new transactions or blocks to neighbours, who forward them onward.
A node's pool of valid transactions waiting to be put into a block.
The block a miner or validator is trying to make acceptable to the network.
The rules and process by which nodes agree on one ordered history.
All correct nodes decide on the same block or value.
The agreed value must satisfy the protocol's rules.
Every correct node eventually reaches a decision.
A faulty node that may lie, stay silent, or send conflicting messages.
A faulty node that simply stops and sends nothing further.
One entity creates many fake identities to gain influence.
Nodes exchange votes and decide when a quorum agrees.
A node shows costly or locked resources to earn the right to propose.
Nodes take turns in a fixed order to propose blocks.
Once a block is final, it cannot be reversed by the protocol.
A block becomes harder to reverse as more blocks build on it.
A block is accepted only after finding a hash below a target.
A validator's chance to propose is proportional to locked coins.
A node waits for a random timer and the first to finish proposes.
A split in the chain; soft forks stay compatible, hard forks do not.

takeaways: Blockchain nodes form a serverless peer-to-peer overlay and discover peers through seed nodes, known addresses, or gossip.
Gossip spreads each transaction and block quickly, but nodes filter duplicates and validate before forwarding.
A transaction moves from wallet to mempool to candidate block to mined block, and the miner earns fees and block reward for ordering.
Consensus must keep agreement, validity, and termination even when nodes crash or behave dishonestly.
Voting-based consensus gives fast finality in a known validator set; proof-based consensus works in open networks with Sybil resistance.
Proof of Work secures history by cost: miners search a nonce for a hash below target, and difficulty adjusts to keep block time steady.
Proof of Stake replaces hash power with locked stake; slashing makes attacks costly but can concentrate power among large holders.
Proof of Elapsed Time and round robin suit permissioned chains where identities are known and energy cost matters.
A soft fork tightens rules while old nodes still accept new blocks; a hard fork changes rules so old and new nodes reject each other.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for clear definitions, a diagram of message or block flow, and a comparison of security, energy, finality, and permissioning across consensus mechanisms.

bank.q: Explain the architecture of a peer-to-peer blockchain network and how a new node discovers peers and receives transactions.
outline: equal nodes with no central server
discovery using seed nodes, known addresses, and gossip

bank.q: Describe the life cycle of a blockchain transaction from wallet creation to confirmation, and state the role of miners.
outline: miner selects transactions into a candidate block

bank.q: Define consensus and explain agreement, validity, and termination. Distinguish crash faults from Byzantine faults.
outline: open networks need Byzantine fault tolerance

bank.q: Compare voting-based and proof-based consensus, and explain deterministic versus probabilistic finality.
outline: voting uses a quorum in a known set
proof uses work or stake in an open set
finality means a block cannot be reversed
deterministic finality is permanent by protocol
probabilistic finality improves with block depth

bank.q: Explain Proof of Work mining: nonce, target, difficulty adjustment, and the 51% attacker.
outline: difficulty retarget keeps block interval steady
heaviest or longest valid chain rule
51% attacker can double spend or censor

bank.q: Explain Proof of Stake: validator selection, stake, slashing, and its differences from Proof of Work.
outline: stake is locked as a bond
selection chance is proportional to stake

bank.q: Explain Proof of Elapsed Time and round-robin consensus, and state where each fits.
outline: Proof of Elapsed Time uses a random wait
round robin uses fixed turn order
known validator set reduces Sybil risk
low energy but liveness risk if leader fails

bank.q: Distinguish soft forks and hard forks, and explain how old nodes behave in each case.
outline: fork is a divergence in the chain
old nodes accept new soft-fork blocks

bank.q: A five-node network receives two conflicting transactions from one wallet. Trace how gossip, mempool policy, and miner choice decide which transaction enters the next block.
outline: mempool may hold both or replace by fee
first confirmed spend makes the other invalid

bank.q: A chain targets one block every 10 minutes. Explain how the network changes difficulty when blocks arrive too fast, and why this protects block interval.
Design a permissioned blockchain for a bank consortium of ten known members. Choose Proof of Elapsed Time or round robin, and justify the choice with fault and liveness concerns.
outline: round robin is simple and fair
Proof of Elapsed Time gives a random leader

bank.q: A protocol change adds a new opcode and causes new nodes to reject blocks from old nodes. Classify the fork and outline a safe migration plan.
Compare Proof of Work, Proof of Stake, Proof of Elapsed Time, and round robin on security, energy use, finality, and permissioning. Recommend one for a supply-chain consortium and defend the choice.
outline: Proof of Work is open and costly
Proof of Stake uses locked stake and slashing
Proof of Elapsed Time needs a trusted timer
round robin needs a known set

bank.q: Evaluate the claim 'Proof of Stake is always better than Proof of Work' using decentralization, attack cost, finality, and bootstrapping.
outline: energy argument favours Proof of Stake

glossary.def: A block a miner or validator is assembling and trying to make acceptable to the network.
The protocol rules and process that make independent nodes agree on one ordered history.
A fault in which a node stops working and sends no further messages.
A fault in which a node may lie, omit messages, or send conflicting messages.
A guarantee that a finalised block cannot be reversed by the protocol.
A measure of how low the Proof of Work target is, adjusted to keep block time steady.
A divergence in the blockchain, either temporary or permanent.
A spreading method where each node forwards new data to its neighbours.
A rule change that makes new blocks invalid to old nodes, often splitting the chain.
A node's local pool of valid but unconfirmed transactions.
A node that selects transactions and performs Proof of Work to produce a block.
The process by which a node learns the addresses of peers and joins the overlay.
A variable number a miner changes to search for a valid Proof of Work hash.
A network of equal nodes that exchange data directly without a central server.
A consensus method where nodes wait for a random timer and the first to finish proposes.
A consensus method where validators lock coins and propose blocks in proportion to stake.
A consensus method where a block requires a hash below a target.
A finality model where reversal becomes less likely as more blocks are added.
A turn-taking rule where nodes propose blocks in a fixed order.
A Proof of Stake penalty that destroys part of a validator's locked coins for misbehaviour.
A rule tightening that old nodes still accept as valid.
Coins locked by a validator as a bond in Proof of Stake.
An attack where one entity creates many fake identities to gain influence.
The threshold value that a Proof of Work block hash must be below.
A node that proposes or attests blocks under Proof of Stake.
An attack where one entity controls most mining power or stake and can reorder or censor blocks.
